entry.summary: Lately, Courtney Werner has been involved with an impressively large percentage of the brilliant experimental folk music coming out of the American south. The sound artist and fiddle player is in Magic Tuber Stringband, Dowsers, and Weirs, which means I’ve been posting quite a bit of her output over the past year and change. Time…
entry.content:
Lately, Courtney Werner has been involved with an impressively large percentage of the brilliant experimental folk music coming out of the American south. The sound artist and fiddle player is in Magic Tuber Stringband, Dowsers, and Weirs, which means I've been posting quite a bit of her output over the past year and change. Time to post some more!

This week Werner announced her debut solo album Tritium Forests. It's coming out on Thrill Jockey in February, and it finds her continuing to blur the line between music and her other career as an ecologist. Lead single "sierra one whiskey eight," for instance, was inspired by recordings of coyotes, barred owls, and whip-poor-wills in what our man Jeff Tweedy once called the Bible-black pre-dawn. "I tried to imagine myself as another voice in the soundscape, responding to and communicating with the calls," Werner says.

The finished track is haunting and magnificent, like Deliverance via claire rousay. Listen below.

02 "sierra one whiskey eight"

04 "sierra six whiskey four"

entry.title: U2 Praise Cameron Winter, Lambrini Girls, & Fontaines D.C.
entry.summary: Mere hours from now, U2 will release Carnaval De Luz, their first album of new material in nine years. As part of the promotional blitz, the band has spoken to NME, sharing praise for a new generation of alt-rockers. Specifically, the Edge loves the politically charged Brighton punk band Lambrini Girls: “I’m just so jealous…
entry.content:
Mere hours from now, U2 will release Carnaval De Luz, their first album of new material in nine years. As part of the promotional blitz, the band has spoken to NME, sharing praise for a new generation of alt-rockers. Specifically, the Edge loves the politically charged Brighton punk band Lambrini Girls: "I’m just so jealous of them. Now that’s a sound I would love to hear on a U2 album. Just the sonics are fantastic." He's also a Geese fan, naturally: "I love what they’re doing, and Cameron Winter’s solo stuff as well. Did you see him on Jimmy Kimmel when he played ‘Drinking Age’? Wow."

Bono, too, has thoughts on Mr. Winter:

He’s the man who understands the power of a silhouette. An original silhouette only comes along every 10 or 20 years. I went to see Geese and he was standing with his back to us. He knows about shadows. The band were going at it like Cookie Monster from Sesame Street, the drummer was incredible, but he was pulling some shapes. As a shape-puller, I appreciated that.

As for their fellow Irish stadium-rockers Fontaines D.C., "We're huge fans of theirs," the Edge says. Bono appreciates the way they raise the bar for their peers: "You have to up your game when people step into the room like Fontaines D.C." As someone who wrote a song about Rosalía for the new U2 album, he of course also appreciates Fontaines' Rosalía collab "Where Is Gone?" His comments:

But Grian [Chatten] has got a very unique spirit. Everyone thinks of singers and songwriters as going around with a diviner, but I think the reason you’re drawn to certain music is like that and you then explain it to yourself later. They just work very well together that band, they’ve got something extraordinary. That was a great song they did with Rosalía.

Carnaval De Luz features the late Dolly Parton's final recording, a duet called "Torn." A country remix of the song by Kent Wells was serviced to radio stations today, and Good Morning America broadcasted an excerpt:

Parton's Instagram account shared a note she wrote to Bono about her work on the song, dated June 2 of this year. "Hope you like what I did," Parton wrote. "I did quite a few things. Take from it what you want and what you need, but I love the song, and I think it could be something really special. Thanks for including me in your life. I've always loved you and always will." Look at Dolly Parton posthumously bringing a tear to my eye!

But wait, there's more! U2 played an intimate show at London's Tate Modern for the BBC last week, and today the first official video from that gig has emerged. The BBC has shared footage of U2 performing "The Greatest Show On Earth," by far the best single from Carnaval De Luz so far. You can watch that below.

Carnaval De Luz is out 11/13 on Island.

entry.title: Mass Text Announce New Album Perfect New Knife: Hear “Pink Slips”
entry.summary: More bands should be influenced by Liars. That’s my first takeaway from “Pink Slips,” a song that is definitely descended from Angus Andrew’s experimental post-punk project. It’s the lead single from Perfect New Knife, the forthcoming album from Chicago’s own Mass Text. Billed as a collective, Mass Text are headed up by Chris Sutter, who…
entry.content:
More bands should be influenced by Liars. That's my first takeaway from "Pink Slips," a song that is definitely descended from Angus Andrew's experimental post-punk project. It's the lead single from Perfect New Knife, the forthcoming album from Chicago's own Mass Text.

Billed as a collective, Mass Text are headed up by Chris Sutter, who also makes raucous punk rock (Hot Snakes meets PUP, I called it) in the band Meat Wave. Perfect New Knife was produced by Dehd's Jason Balla, who released his debut solo album as Accessory this year. The droning, ominous "Pink Slips" works as a wondrous introduction to the album, especially when Sutter quotes the Partridge Family's "I Think I Love You" in dark, deranged fashion on the second verse.

Sutter shared this statement:

"Pink Slips" is the starting point and impetus for Perfect New Knife. While it doesn’t really sound like any other song on the album, it gave us the freedom to produce whatever felt right for the record, depending on the song and energy we wanted to convey. We built on top of the home demo in the studio, so many of the original takes and much of the feeling of the song were retained. The feedback on the track is from two really old walkie-talkies that I recorded on my phone while on tour. The term ‘pink slips’ refers to a time when my gums wouldn’t stop bleeding, so all my teeth looked like little pink slips in my mouth.

Listen below.

entry.title: Michael Rapaport Cosigns “Dope New Group” Yeah Yeah Yeahs, Karen O Shares New Solo Song “Soft Machine”
entry.summary: Michael Rapaport would like to tell you about a “dope new group” called Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Rapaport, the actor, comedian, and podcaster, went viral on Wednesday for an Instagram video in which he raves about “Maps,” his latest musical discovery. “Yo, you ever heard of this group called the Yeah Yeah Yeahs?” he asks, with…
entry.content:
Michael Rapaport would like to tell you about a "dope new group" called Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Rapaport, the actor, comedian, and podcaster, went viral on Wednesday for an Instagram video in which he raves about "Maps," his latest musical discovery.

"Yo, you ever heard of this group called the Yeah Yeah Yeahs?" he asks, with a photo of YYYs vocalist Karen O superimposed over the footage. "I don't really like a lot of new music," Rapaport continues, "but I just heard the Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Great song, this song 'Maps.' Fantastic! I've been playing it all day. I guess the lead singer's name is Karen something."

It would seem that Rapaport, a New York City native who directed a documentary about A Tribe Called Quest, must be trolling. There's no way he lived through the last quarter-century without becoming aware of this world-famous band from his hometown or encountering their signature song, released in 2003. But if he's joking, he keeps a straight face as he proceeds. "Cause mostly I like older music, my hip-hop, my old soul, jazz. I don't know about the new music. But this 'Maps,' something 'Y' something, Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Dope new group, you should check 'em out." It's called "Y Control," Michael, and we appreciate you pointing it out.

In Rapaport's defense, the distinction between old and new music has mostly been eradicated in the TikTok and Spotify era. As discussed in our Coachella poster breakdown, which highlighted Weezer's enduring popularity, young people today don't seem to much care when a song came out. Yeah Yeah Yeahs have certainly benefitted from this phenomenon. "Maps" went viral in 2024, which sent the song rocketing up the streaming charts and probably contributed to Rolling Stone's recent decision to name it the greatest rock song of the 21st century so far. But Rapaport's been around. He should know!

In other other YYYs news, Karen O has a new solo song called "Soft Machine" in Space Cadet, the new animated adaptation of turntablist Kid Koala's 2011 graphic novel. The movie, which features no dialogue, debuted last year at the Berlin International Film Festival. It follows the astronaut Celeste as she embarks on her first solo mission into space, leaving behind Robot, the Guardianbot who raised her. Kid Koala, who also composed the film's original score, has called it "a tomorrow-days lullaby about finding your place in the universe."

"Soft Machine" finds Karen O in sparse, intimate ballad mode. A one-minute excerpt of the song can be heard in "Empty Nester," a clip featuring Robot that premiered at Billboard:

Space Cadet premieres this weekend. Tickets are available here. In September, Yeah Yeah Yeahs released Hidden In Pieces: Live At The Royal Albert Hall, a live album recorded over two nights at the storied London venue last year, with bonus recordings from San Diego, Chicago, New York, and Mexico City. Stream it below if you're looking for a good time.

There's also a companion short film by Barnaby Clay:

Somewhere in there, she also made her auspicious acting debut, playing Magick, a stripper in a bedazzled neck brace, on the final season of Euphoria. She wasn’t…
entry.content:
Rosalía has had a busy year since the release of her astonishing 2025 album LUX: a global arena tour, a Saturday Night Live performance, a Fontaines D.C. duet. Somewhere in there, she also made her auspicious acting debut, playing Magick, a stripper in a bedazzled neck brace, on the final season of Euphoria. She wasn't on the show all that much, but she made an impression. Now. Rosalía has lined up another high-profile acting role.

According to The Hollywood Reporter, Rosalía is part of the starry cast of Wet, the new film from Alma Ha'rel, director of Honey Boy and the Apple TV+ miniseries Lady In The Lake. The Wet cast also includes Connor Storrie, Rebecca Ferguson, Odessa A’zion, Javier Bardem, and Lukas Haas. That's a great cast! Ha'rel co-wrote the film with Christian Stangeby, and Lionsgate will distribute it in North America and the UK. We don't know any of the story details yet, but Ha'rel has made a statement about it:

Lately, I’ve had to find humor in chaos and humanity in the most unpredictable situations. I’m grateful to Lionsgate for embracing a film that speaks to this wild moment in time. I’m incredibly excited to bring this remarkable group of actors together and make a film that refuses to behave.

Production is set to begin in January in the Dominican Republic.

In September, he released the standalone single “The Devil,” his first music in a couple of years. He followed it with “Yesterday’s Tomorrow” last month, and now he’s got a…
entry.content:
The LA musician John Rossiter makes weird, idiosyncratic indie rock under the name Young Jesus, and he's on a bit of a run right now. In September, he released the standalone single "The Devil," his first music in a couple of years. He followed it with "Yesterday's Tomorrow" last month, and now he's got a wild new track called "Boulevard."

"Boulevard" is Young Jesus getting funky. The track has a vaguely bluesy classic rock intensity, and it's driven by a monster country-funk bass-groove. Rossiter sometimes belts his words out in a heartfelt warble, and he sometimes warbles them in Auto-Tuned falsetto. It's one of those tracks where you can pick out tons of ingredients without being able to figure out why it works the way that it does. Listen below.

"Boulevard" is out now on Music Sounds/Saddle Creek.

entry.title: Mynolia – “Dragon”
entry.summary: A couple of weeks into the new year, the Nashville-based indie-folk singer-songwriter Mynolia will release her full-length debut Salt Around My Bed. We’ve already posted the early singles “Holy Line” and “Take The Mountain By Surprise.” But the track that has impressed me most is “Dragon,” which she released yesterday. It’s a still, hypnotic reverie…
entry.content:
A couple of weeks into the new year, the Nashville-based indie-folk singer-songwriter Mynolia will release her full-length debut Salt Around My Bed. We've already posted the early singles "Holy Line" and "Take The Mountain By Surprise." But the track that has impressed me most is "Dragon," which she released yesterday. It's a still, hypnotic reverie built from acoustic guitars and psychedelic flutes, and it reminds me of early Beth Orton, which I mean as high praise. Here's what Mynolia says about it:

This song is really about finding something you didn’t know you were missing. If "Holy Line" is unknowingly dreaming about it, "Dragon" is about unavoidably living it. “Never thought I’d be seen hiding between the trees. It’s a tumble I know from forever ago. Like the old folks have told, stories ancient as dragons.

When something finds you even while you’re actively hiding from it, it can feel pretty cosmic. The path is clear and has to be taken, it feels familiar and large somehow, like an epic folktale. I loved how this track evolved, from home recording and organic shuffle drums by Florian Holoubek to synth swells by Rich Ruth, horns by Corin Droullard and flute by Sam Que. This was another of the first few I recorded, so it would get worked on and added to, then put on the shelf for months at a time. Lyrically, the first verse and last are like the bookends of a significant chapter of my life, one of unburdening, embracing chance, and change and leaping into the unknown.

Check it out below.

Salt Around My Bed is out 1/15 on Full Time Hobby.

entry.title: Weird Nightmare – “Buzzing In My Head”
entry.summary: Former METZ frontman Alex Edkins is now half of the duo Noble Rot, and he also makes his own fiery, propulsive power-pop jams under the name Weird Nightmare. One indication that Weird Nightmare is real-deal power-pop: A lot of their best songs never show up on albums. Earlier this year, Weird Nightmare released Hoopla, an…
entry.content:
Former METZ frontman Alex Edkins is now half of the duo Noble Rot, and he also makes his own fiery, propulsive power-pop jams under the name Weird Nightmare. One indication that Weird Nightmare is real-deal power-pop: A lot of their best songs never show up on albums. Earlier this year, Weird Nightmare released Hoopla, an LP that Edkins co-produced with Spoon's Jim Eno. It ruled. Now, there's a new standalone Weird Nightmare single that's right up there with anything on the album.

Weird Nightmare's new song "Buzzing In My Head" has a mighty sha-la-la riff and a yelpy and heartsick vocal. When it hits the chorus, the harmonies go so hard that they almost glow. Edkins recorded the song with Holy Fuck's Graham Walsh, his partner in Noble Rot, on production. It's got the same backing musicians who played on Hoopla: Loel Campbell on drums and Matthew Kuester on bass.

In a press release, Edkins says, "'Buzzing In My Head’ is about that one person/place/thing/memory/experience that never really leaves your waking mind. It stays with you to the point of distraction and overwhelms your ability to complete menial tasks." Check out the song and the dates for Weird Nightmare's brief upcoming tour below.

entry.title: Duran Duran’s Roger Taylor Announces Retirement
entry.summary: Roger Taylor is stepping down. Duran Duran’s founding drummer announced his retirement from the band today, ending a run that saw him provide the backbeat for myriad classics and landed him in the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame. In a statement on the band’s website and socials, Taylor, 66, reveals that he was recently…
entry.content:
Roger Taylor is stepping down. Duran Duran's founding drummer announced his retirement from the band today, ending a run that saw him provide the backbeat for myriad classics and landed him in the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame. In a statement on the band's website and socials, Taylor, 66, reveals that he was recently diagnosed with tinnitus, and the worsening of the condition precipitated his exit from the group.

Here's his statement:

This is one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever had to make. Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I’ll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they’ve shown us over the years. But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse, and I’ve reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors.

Figuring out the timing of all of this has not been easy, but I’m going out on a real high. We’ve just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour, which followed our second headline show at BST Hyde Park, our induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, and a return to the studio with Nile Rodgers. I couldn’t have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I’ll treasure forever. I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John.

Duran Duran are one of the defining acts of the new wave era, emerging from the UK post-punk landscape with a sleek, stylish dance-rock sound and a fantastically glammy look that made them fixtures of early MTV. Taylor became the band's first drummer in 1979, performing on the band's first three albums as they rose to global fame. He left the group in 1985 after Duran Duran's performance at Live Aid, the massive international charity concert, citing weariness with fame and the band's demanding schedule. Taylor rejoined the lineup in 2001 as Duran Duran reassembled the lineup from 1982's Rio and commenced a massively successful reunion tour. He has remained behind the kit up until now.

entry.title: Teenage Halloween – “Standing On The Corner”
entry.summary: New Jersey pop-punk tunesmiths Teenage Halloween released Till You Return, their most recent album, just before Halloween 2023. This made sense. Today, the band returns with a brand new single, their first in the three years since that album came out. Except this time, the record is arriving just after Halloween — a real plot…
entry.content:
New Jersey pop-punk tunesmiths Teenage Halloween released Till You Return, their most recent album, just before Halloween 2023. This made sense. Today, the band returns with a brand new single, their first in the three years since that album came out. Except this time, the record is arriving just after Halloween — a real plot twist from this band.

As far as I can tell, Teenage Halloween's new song "Standing On The Corner" has nothing to do with the New York avant-jazz crew Standing On The Corner, though that group should obviously make a song called "Teenage Halloween" now. I'm pretty sure the triumphant chorus is about literally standing on a literal corner, though I guess it could be about metaphorically standing on a metaphorical corner: "I was standing on the corner/ I was waiting for the train/ There are paths that we all choose/ They’re not real without pain."

The song is a charged-up, ultra-catchy singalong anthem about self-doubt and the need for progress. The members of Teenage Halloween don't all live in New Jersey anymore, but they kept it real Jersey on this one, recording in their home state with Bouncing Souls/Gaslight Anthem producer Erik Kase Romero. In a press release, singer/guitarist Luk Henderiks says, "'Standing On The Corner' is about taking on challenges head first and redirecting anxious energy into hope. This is a song built on a moment of change, encapsulated by a decision to leave a suburban past and dive into city life." Check it out below.

entry.title: “Flava In Ya Ear” Sample Finally Identified After 32 Years
entry.summary: The first release ever to come out on Bad Boy Records was “Flava In Ya Ear,” the late Long Island rapper Craig Mack’s 1994 debut single. It’s a classic piece of ’90s New York rap expressionism, driven by a dusty boom-bap beat from the great producer Easy Mo Bee. It quickly became a huge crossover…
entry.content:
The first release ever to come out on Bad Boy Records was "Flava In Ya Ear," the late Long Island rapper Craig Mack's 1994 debut single. It's a classic piece of '90s New York rap expressionism, driven by a dusty boom-bap beat from the great producer Easy Mo Bee. It quickly became a huge crossover hit, reaching #9 on the Billboard Hot 100. As someone who was in ninth grade when the track came out, I heard it all the time.

These days, "Flava In Ya Ear" is even better-known for its iconic posse-cut remix. Biggie Smalls opened that remix, and his endlessly quotable verse was a key part of his rise. LL Cool J, Busta Rhymes, and Rampage also appeared on the remix, and the Hype Williams-directed video is one of the key documents of its era. Craig Mack passed away in 2018 at the age of 46, and "Flava In Ya Ear" was his defining legacy.

Easy Mo Bee's "Flava In Ya Ear" beat is driven by what I always though was a detuned two-note horn riff. I was wrong. In a 2014 Youtube interview, Easy Mo Bee said that he made that beat in his underwear after waking up one morning, using a stack of records that he'd bought the day before, and that the riff was "a guitar, but with a lot of reverb, a huge throw of reverb. But it carries the song. You would think that you need all of these big, busy elements for a melody to carry the song. That, those two notes, that was the melody. That's what carried the song, and everything else was built around that."

Nobody had ever positively identified the record that Easy Mo Bee sampled for those two notes. Back then, rap producers took care in disguising the samples that they chopped up, making them difficult to trace — not just for legal reasons, but as part of the art. Recently, though, a YouTuber who goes by the name ShakerMaker has been uploading discoveries from the Sample Sanctuary Discord, and they have evidently figured out the source of the "Flava In Ya Ear."

According to these folks, the "Flava In Ya Ear" beat uses two isolated guitar notes from the jazz guitarist Melvin Sparks' 1971 version of the 1932 Broadway standard "Alone Together." Apparently, those two notes come from the middle of a solo, and they have been slowed down and blasted with effects until they're completely unrecognizable.

The people in the same Discord also claim that they recently figured out a previously undiscovered sample from Stardust's 1998 house classic "Music Sounds Better With You."

I'm fascinated by the way some people can listen to music. How do you figure out how to turn that sample into the "Flava In Ya Ear" beat? And then, how do you find it, decades later?

entry.content:
Stop what you're doing. Take a moment to relax with this one. If you're a fan of the current wave of alt-country, NPR Americana, chilled-out heartland rock, indie dad rock, or whatever else you want to call it, you gotta check out "Lucky Ones" by Bonny Doon.

You may be familiar with the Detroit band from their many years of service in the indie rock trenches, or for their stint as Katie Crutchfield's Saint Cloud backing band, helping to usher in Waxahatchee's alt-country era. If not, it's time to tap in with Forever Green, their new album coming in February on ANTI-.

Bonny Doon mostly made the album in Arizona with Austin Owen and Francis Bartolomeo. It also has the band's 2024 single "Clock Keeps Ticking," produced by Sam Cohen, and Kevin Basko handled some additional recording. The immaculately downtrodden "Lucky Ones" is a great introduction (or reintroduction) to the band, marked by Bill Lennox's tender, plaintive vocals and a dazzling array of guitars. "I wonder how it feels to be one of the lucky ones," he sings on the chorus, between bouts of exquisite slide guitar that carry upward like prayers.

A word from Lennox:

Most people scrape by and can barely afford to live despite working their ass off. Meanwhile the rich get richer and those in power are doing everything they can to suppress the rights and dignity of working-class people. It’s kind of a culmination of grievance and frustration both personal and collective. In my case, 12 years into a band, 12 years older, still bartending until 3am, the body doesn’t recover like it used to. You can sometimes feel like your dues have been paid, and you’re waiting on something to get easier or fall into place. I know a lot of people that feel like that.

Listen below.

entry.title: Yella Beezy Gets Life In Prison For Hiring Hitman To Kill Rival Rapper MO3
entry.summary: The Dallas rapper Yella Beezy has been found guilty of capital murder and sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. As the Associated Press reports, a jury in Dallas County unanimously found the 35-year-old rapper, whose real name is Markles Conway, guilty of hiring a hitman to kill rival Dallas rapper MO3…
entry.content:
The Dallas rapper Yella Beezy has been found guilty of capital murder and sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. As the Associated Press reports, a jury in Dallas County unanimously found the 35-year-old rapper, whose real name is Markles Conway, guilty of hiring a hitman to kill rival Dallas rapper MO3 in 2020. MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble, was shot dead in 2020 at the age of 28. The jury found against Yella Beezy on the sixth anniversary of MO3's death.

In the trial, prosecutors claimed that the murder was the result of a years-long rap feud between Yella Beezy and MO3 and that Beezy paid a man named Kewon White $40,000 to kill him. White was found guilty of capital murder in September, and he got the same sentence of life without the possibility of parole. Yella Beezy was arrested for the murder in 2025.

According to prosecutors, MO3 was driving down a Dallas highway in the middle of the day in 2020 when White pulled up next to him, got out of the car, and pulled out a gun. MO3 got out of his car and tried to run away, and White fired more than 40 shots at him, hitting and injuring a nearby bystander, who survived. MO3 later died from his wounds in a hospital. Yella Beezy survived a similar highway shooting in 2018, and prosecutors showed jurors a video in which he claimed he would "get his lick back."

Both Yella Beezy and MO3 had successful rap careers prior to the murder. Yella Beezy's 2017 single "That's On Me" went platinum. He released a remix to the track featuring 2 Chainz, T.I., Rich The Kid, Jeezy, and Trapboy Freddy, and it also went platinum and reached #56 on the Billboard Hot 100. In 2019, he reached #78 with "Bacc At It Again," a Quavo/Gucci Mane collab that went gold. His most recent album Bad Azz Yella Boy came out in 2022, and he released the single "Where I Been" in September. MO3 had two double platinum singles, the 2020 Kevin Gates collab "Broken Love" and the posthumous 2021 "Outside" remix, featuring OG Bobby Billions. His posthumous 2021 album Shottaz 4Eva went gold.

entry.title: Index – “Heartbeat Glitch”
entry.summary: Index, the electronic hardcore duo of ex-Control Top members, have shared "Heartbeat Glitch," a new song from the 'Vis Intertiae' sessions.
entry.content:
Index, the electronic-inflected hardcore punk band made up of ex-Control Top members Alan Creedon and Alex Lichtenauer, just released their debut album Vis Inertiae in September. They recorded the LP with Arthur Rizk, the in-demand producer for music on the heavy spectrum from Prurient and Power Trip, at Show Me The Body's Corpus studio. And now we're getting one more track from those sessions, the bashed-out "Heartbeat Glitch."

"I think the first thing Arthur said to us was, 'We've got to accent the '90s breakbeat Aphex Twin vibe of your band,'" Creedon says of the recording process with Rizk. "And we did. It's not obvious at all times, but there are extra little hi-hat glitches and hybrid kits happening with weird layering. That's something that we really wanted to be, this hardcore band with one foot in electronic music."

Listen to "Heartbeat Glitch" below.

entry.title: 19 Thoughts On The Coachella 2027 Poster
entry.summary: How are we supposed to feel right now? What is the effect supposed to be? When the powerhouse booking company Goldenvoice unveils the lineup for their next Coachella Music & Arts Festival, how do they expect the world to react? The deluge of names always overwhelms, even when it underwhelms. It always has a few…
entry.content:
How are we supposed to feel right now? What is the effect supposed to be? When the powerhouse booking company Goldenvoice unveils the lineup for their next Coachella Music & Arts Festival, how do they expect the world to react? The deluge of names always overwhelms, even when it underwhelms. It always has a few galactically famous acts and then a bunch of people who you have never heard of in your life. Maybe it's unavoidable, but my big takeaway is that they want you to feel confused. They want you to feel old.

Do you feel old? I feel old, but that's because I am old. I feel old every day. If you're old, Coachella shouldn't be an issue anymore. You're not going to be there. Instead, you have the unbelievably luxurious option of livestreaming the entire festival on YouTube. You can flip around between things happening in real time, and you don't even have to deal with the long hikes in between stages. It's great. You can learn a lot of things watching those streams.

You will have to learn those things, though, because every Coachella lineup necessarily includes a whole bunch of acts whose names will be absolutely unfamiliar to you. This is part of the game. You have to accept it. You can't possibly keep tabs on every ascending and descending name in the worlds of EDM, K-pop, emo, reggaeton, hyperpop, rage rap, and whatever other subgenre might be cool this year. Nobody can. It's a fool's errand. Don't try. You should be confused.

Nevertheless, the main reaction that I see to every Coachella lineup announcement is a kind of theatrical eye-rolling exasperation. People are like: This? This is what they're giving us? I'm not strawmanning here. More and more often, this is my reaction. Why? What's wrong with me?

I'm not going to Coachella. I went once, more than a decade ago, and now I watch every festival stream on my laptop. Nobody's ripping me off. Also, every Coachella lineup has a ton of stuff that I like. If you did go to the festival, you could easily find three days' worth of acts that would blow your shit back. That's true of the 2027 lineup, too. If you can't find a ton of cool shit, then the real inescapable conclusion is that you don't like that much music.

But this annual column isn't really about Coachella itself. Instead, it's about the poster — the placements, the font sizes, and the stories that they tell. I have been writing versions of this piece every year for a long, long time. I have watched people climb up the poster and then fall back down.

The thing that I love about the Coachella poster is that it lays everything out in stark, hierarchical terms. Some acts are bigger than other acts. Some festivals don't want you to know that. They'll list out all the artists alphabetically, or they'll organize them into different tiers or stages. Not Coachella. If two acts are playing the same day at Coachella, then one of them is going to be listed higher than the other. There are winners, and there are losers. There's no focus on any particular vibe or genre here. Coachella does not narrowcast. If you are on the Coachella poster, then the people at Goldenvoice have deemed you to be part of the conversation. When the poster drops, you know exactly where you stand.

The Coachella poster is not an organic document. Artists tend to invest a lot of feelings in where they might sit on a Coachella poster, and their teams care even more deeply. I'm sure artists turn down Coachella bookings because they can't stand to be listed in the fourth line when they think they should be in the third. We rarely get to see any of those negotiations. Though we did get some leaks this year, the final document comes to us like tablets carried down from the mountaintop. This is who's on top, who matters. It's up to us to parse what that means.

So let's do that. Let's get into a Coachella-poster close read and parse out some of the stories that it tells. It's an annual tradition. It's what we have to do. You can just look at the Coachella poster and get frustrated, if you want. For me, though, it's a whole lot more fun to get lost in the weeds. What follows is one old man's take on what next year's poster tells us.

1. The headliners are booooring. We knew this. It's not a surprise. Back in September, Tame Impala and Dua Lipa were both reported to be headlining Coachella, with SZA jumping on board in October. Because of the reports about those headliners, we've also seen a ton of unconfirmed stories about the headliners that Goldenvoice tried and failed to book — Rage Against The Machine, Miley Cyrus, BTS, Radiohead, Oasis. All of those acts would've been big swings, and all of them evidently said no. Instead, we're left with a tremendously safe trio.

In isolation, Tame Impala, Dua Lipa, and SZA all make perfect sense as Coachella headliners. They're all big names. They all have hits. They're all culturally present. They're all fully established, and you could argue that all of them are at or near their peaks. They're neither young nor old. Tame Impala's Kevin Parker is 40. SZA is 37. Dua Lipa is 31. Tame Impala has worked with both Dua Lipa and SZA, which means there's a high likelihood of crossover moments.

I'd have fun watching all three headliners. I have had fun watching two of the three; Lipa is the only one I've never seen live. Tame Impala and SZA have both played multiple Coachellas, and Tame have headlined before, though they're riding a new peak since "Dracula" blew up. Lipa has never played the festival, but that's kind of a surprise. I'm sure she'll be great.

But none of them feel special, do they? There's no real surprise factor. Lipa has taken a few years off from pop stardom, but she's pretty clearly about to come back to it. All three acts have done big tours in recent memory. They're all used to the spotlight.

Coachella hasn't coaxed any reluctant legends back to the big stage. They haven't figured out a way to channel mass gen-Z nostalgia, like they did when Justin Bieber headlined last year. (Miley Cyrus could've done that.) There's no sense that any of these artists have suddenly elevated themselves to headliner status. We could spend all day listing off possible headliners who might've been more exciting. Olivia Rodrigo and/or Chappell Roan. Arctic Monkeys. Rosalía. The Cure, returning to the desert. The Hole reunion that we'll probably never get. The Daft Punk reunion that we'll definitely never get. Hell, Bruno Mars, why not.

Coachella's reputation depends, at least in part, on holy shit bookings. These are not holy shit headliners. Fortunately, there's plenty of holy shit action in the high undercard.

2. Holy shit! Madonna! Now we're talking. I was in the crowd at Coachella in 2015, when Drake introduced Madonna as a surprise guest, and then she surprised him by shoving her tongue down his throat. When she walked offstage, he wiped his lips off. It was funny.

Madonna is the most famous person on this poster by a good distance. She's arguably our greatest living pop star, and she's got more hits than all three headliners combined. She could've presumably headlined, if she wanted. But the poster specifically tells us that Madonna will be "in the dance tent." This is what she wants us to know.

Back in 2006, Madonna made a surprise appearance in Sahara Tent. It was a big deal. She was promoting Confessions On A Dance Floor, and that was her way of signaling her engagement with yet another generation of ravers. This year, Madonna released Confessions II, and it fucking slaps. She hasn't toured behind that record. I'm guessing that this Coachella appearance will be something like Nine Inch Noize last year — a full-on superstar doing something special that was created with this specific venue in mind. Madonna might not be the headliner, but if I were going to the fest this year, that would be the main event of the whole weekend for me.

3. DA! DEE! YAN! KAAAAAY! And then there's our other bonus headliner. Reggaeton originator Daddy Yankee gets the special spot at the bottom of the poster, and I think that's a lot more interesting than the big dance acts that sometimes get the nod. Yankee did a retirement tour in 2022, but I don't think anyone took that seriously. His '00s hits have persistently refused to disappear from the culture. My kids' Spanish is elementary at best, but both of them love "Gasolina." Coachella is clearly still shooting for global reach, and a huge percentage of the biggest acts in the world right now are directly inspired by what this guy did in the not-too-distant past. A cool booking.

4. Pop music on top. An interesting development that I've been noting in the past few years: A lot of the most exciting music being made right now exists in the realm of straight-up pop. Sometimes, that stuff can get experimental, which is cool. Sometimes, it just goes for endorphin-rush thrills, and that's cool, too. A pop artist doesn't necessarily have to make actual pop hits to tour big venues, though it doesn't hurt.

In his book Major Labels, Kelefa Sanneh noted that people seem to use the term "pure pop music" to refer to stylistic descendants of Madonna, so it's significant that Madonna is on this year's poster. It's just as significant that Dua Lipa, a clear Madonna disciple, is a headliner. A lot of the other exciting acts on this year's lineup fit into the pop category in one way or another: Zara Larsson, Robyn, Adéla, Tove Lo, Haute & Freddy. Remi Wolf and Caroline Polachek are in that mix, too. I'd never heard of After, an LA duo pretty far down the poster, but the couple of tracks that I heard today go hard.

If these artists all go off the way I think they will, Katy Perry might start thinking about another comeback attempt.

5. Glitched-out underground pop gets its spotlight moment. It's hard to say where straight-up pop ends and its various freaked-out online variants begin. But this year's Coachella is awfully heavy on a certain strain of debauched, hedonistic, static-addled internet music. Most of those cult heroes are in the smaller lines, but look at Snow Strippers, back for the second year in a row and all the way up there in line three.

Snow Strippers have a proven festival track record. But a lot of the other hyperpop acts on this year's lineup are new to the idea of playing shows at all. They're here on energy, on swirling vibes. Some of them will probably shit the bed. Others might achieve transcendence. It's time for people like Shygirl, underscores, the Hellp, Bassvictim, Tiffany Day, ear, and rommulas to show the world what they can do. Maybe I should mention Drain Gang, Nettspend, and xaviersobased here, too, since there's not exactly a firm border between hyperpop and brainrotted rage rap these days.

6. K-pop, plus the rest of the world. At this point, Coachella is part of the K-pop promotional machine. When K-pop acts play the festival, it's a big deal. Blackpink's 2019 set got a ton of attention, and then they (technically) headlined in 2023. That's probably why Jisoo, the least interesting solo Blackpink member, is so far up near the top of this year's poster. There's other K-pop at the top, too. Babymonster are a YG Entertainment girl group who just debuted in 2024. And then there's NCT, a baffling interlinked network of seven different boy bands. There are 23 different guys in NCT across all of those groups. They're like the K-pop Wu-Tang, where it just looks like absolute chaos if you're not all the way plugged in. Are they all going to be there?

I've spent the entire day digging through the names on the festival poster that I didn't already know. Most of them are dance DJs, but some of them are pop acts from different parts of the world, and I'm happy to learn of their existence. For instance: Where you aware of SB19, a K-pop-style idol group from the Philippines? I was not. I'm fascinated.

There's so much stuff from all around the world on this lineup, Daddy Yankee being only the most obvious and immediate example. There's a lot more, too. Becky G is American, but she's part of what Yankee started. So are Argentina's Milo J, Spain's Bad Gyal, and Chile's Akriila, though none of them sound anything like each other. (Honestly, Akriila is at least as much hyperpop as she is reggaeton.)

Punjabi star Diljit Dosanjh has played Coachella before, and his set looked crazy. The chaotic Japanese girl group ATARASHI GAKKO! are back for a second round, too. Ayra Starr is this year's designated Afrobeats representative. Los Pibes Chorros, from Argentina, belong to the subgenre of cumbia villera — raw, stripped-down cumbia, at least from what I'm reading right now. The slinky girl group no na follow the K-pop blueprint, but they're from Indonesia.

People used to talk about how you should go see any Australian band play Coachella. Historically, lots and lots of Australians come out to the festival and then go fucking nuts for their own stars. Now, people come to Coachella from all over the world, and they do the same thing. One of my favorite things about this year's lineup is the way it offers so many radically different versions of that spectacle.

7. A big year for R&B. Plenty of past Coachella headliners have been R&B singers, or singers with heavy R&B influences — Prince, Beyoncé, Childish Gambino, Frank Ocean, the Weeknd, Ariana Grande, Justin Bieber. From that perspective, it's not at all surprising to see SZA as a headliner. But I'm not sure I've ever seen a previous Coachella lineup where R&B overshadows rap. This poster also has Steve Lacy, Kehlani, Victoria Monét, Leon Thomas, Mariah The Scientist, Jorja Smith, Kelela, Odeal, the Womack Sisters — artists who don't necessarily have much in common, but who could all be considered R&B singers in one sense or another. That's pretty striking!

8. Rap is maybe not in crisis anymore. Last year, I was lightly shocked at the relative lack of rap on the Coachella lineup. This year's selection is arguably paltry and certainly chaotic, but it feels a bit more robust. Don Toliver, who recently graduated to arena status, is probably the biggest newish rap star to come along in the past few years. He's in the immediate support slot this year, and I wouldn't be shocked if he's a headliner somewhere down the line. His music doesn't compel me at all, but I might stream his set anyway. I bet it'll be something to see.

The rest of this year's rap selection is all over the fucking place, though I can't help but notice that a lot of them are white guys. Someone should really follow Mike D around with a camera and record his reactions to EsDeeKid and Nettspend, his distant descendants in the white-rapper lineage. Drain Gang, history's greatest Swedish rap crew, have prominent billing. (They're not all white, but they are Swedish.) Beyond the slightly uncomfortable race factor, I'm into the idea of Freddie Gibbs, xaviersobased, Fetty Wap, and Genesis Owusu, plus all those white and/or Swedish guys, representing the genre in vastly, discombobulatingly different ways.

9. The Turnstile effect is over. In the past few years, I've been tracking the way that Coachella has treated hardcore. Turnstile have had some big, magic moments at the fest. If they hadn't played last year, they'd probably be on this poster, likely pretty close to the top. But unilke past years, this Coachella has no hardcore bands. I honestly don't get it. I'm not saying chug-mosh bands like Final Resting Place belong at Coachella, but a group like Angel Du$t would probably crush it.

Instead, next year's Coachella has a few of the legacy punk acts that were once Goldenvoice's specialty — the Damned, Social Distortion, and Pennywise, all of which will probably be a lot of fun. And then there's a healthy dollop of emo. Pinegrove, on hiatus for the past few years, are the closest this poster has to a big reunion, which probably accounts for why they're so high up on the poster. Basement and American Football, whose reunions are not new, are in the mix. So are La Dispute.

For me, one of the most exciting bands on the bill is First Day Back, an extremely young '90s-style DIY emo crew who just released the debut album Forward last year. They went from playing basements to big stages very quickly, and it's both shocking and cool to see them already at the Coachella level. I guess that surprise factor makes them this year's equivalent to Drain or Soul Glo or Speed. Maybe the Turnstile effect is something else now.

10. The dream of the '90s is alive. When I was listing off those emo bands, I almost threw Weezer into the mix, just for fun. Even though they've spent decades making some of the worst music you ever heard in your life, Weezer remain hugely powerful. Kids love them. They're way up near the top of this poster, and they're only the second band I've ever seen that evidently warrant their own Coachella-poster font. (The reunited Misfits were the first.)

Speaking anecdotally, my children have come to absolutely fucking love '90s alt-rock. I did not indoctrinate them into those ways. They found that shit via TikTok. That's one of the effects of an internet environment that strips music of its context. Bands aren't old or new anymore. They all exist on the same plane. So when Weezer get booked at Coachella today, it's not because they're trying to convince fortysomethings to buy tickets. They're doing it for the kids.

Plenty of other '90s heroes will also return to the desert next spring: Mike D, Underworld, Pennywise, American Football. Since I Left You technically came out in 2000, but I feel like the Avalanches belong in this category, too. And most intriguingly, motherfucking Enigma will play Coachella. What will that be like? I bet it will rule. I am just now picturing myself stoned in the desert late at night with "Return To Innocence" playing really loud, and I'm wondering if maybe I should go to this festival after all.

11. Nostalgia takes different forms. I love seeing Giorgio Moroder's name on a festival bill, especially one that's this heavy on EDM acts who could've never existed if not for what that guy did. (I guess Moroder is the fest's obligatory film-score composer, too. He does have an Oscar.) But given that all of Moroder's greatest hits are older than any of this year's Coachella headliners, I'm not sure he fully qualifies as a nostalgia act.

Beyond the '90s throwbacks, this Coachella poster has a few acts who call back to moments in the much less distant past — artists whose music might remind people much younger than me of their own pasts. That's my best explanation for why Empire Of The Sun are so high on this bill. Is Fetty Wap there for nostalgia purposes, or just because he's been having a TikTok moment lately? Is there any difference? What about Måneskin? Do the Neighbourhood make teenagers think about when they were eight years old?

What about Martin Garrix and Tiësto, big names of the '00s EDM boom? Are they here for nostalgia or because they're the guys who always play the dance tent? Much to consider.

12. Indie rock...? Phoebe Bridgers is both a real-deal indie rocker and a genuine crossover star. She'll headline a lot of festivals in 2027, and she's also in the immediate support slot at Coachella. I wonder if she was in the headliner conversation there, too. But she's a generational figure, a one of one. The festival has plenty of other indie rockers, but they don't exactly get marquee billing here. Look at This Is Lorelei — universally respected among his peers, the maker of one of this year's finest albums, still way down there in the small print.

Do Angine de Poitrine count as an indie rock band? They're very much their own thing, and the perfect storm of festival-friendly virality still wasn't enough to get them too far up this poster. They're still higher than buzz-band types like Julia Wolf, Twisted Teens, Getdown Services, Chanel Beads, Fat Dog, mary in the junkyard, Lambrini Girls, and Florence Road. Indie rock has its own festivals. At Coachella, it's just a small part of the landscape, and not exactly a priority. I could spend all day naming indie bands that could've played this festival. Maybe I'll do some of that later in this article.

13. Lots of collectives. I already mentioned NCT, the vast K-pop army, and Drain Gang, the Swedish rap crew, but they aren't the only loose confederations on the poster. There's also the UK house label Solid Grooves (pretty high on the poster) and the American DJ crew Close Friends Only. Dinner Party — Kamasi Washington, 9th Wonder, Robert Glasper, and Terrace Martin — might be more of a supergroup than a collective, but maybe that's splitting hairs. I'd guess there's a high probability of guest stars at the Dinner Party set.

14. The wave gets darker. Coachella will always be the place where Peter Murphy led a Bauhaus reunion set while hanging upside down like a bat. Theatrical goth shit belongs there. So it's fun to see stuff like Boy Harsher and Twin Tribes on this poster. I don't think Brutalismus 3000 count as darkwave, exactly, but they also belong in the general "music for the blood rave in Blade" vicinity.

15. Something is happening in dance music. I need to tell a quick story here. Last year, the whole Stereogum staff went out to Barcelona for Primavera. The main-stage area at that festival gets really packed, and I was right in the middle of the crowd for Charli XCX's set. I'm extremely tall, and I felt bad for the girls stuck behind me. After a few songs, I asked them if they'd like to go in front. There was this absolutely stunning woman next to me in the crowd — she was pretty tall, too — and she didn't think I should have to do that. She was like, "Nooo! You were vibeeng!"

I played that interaction over in my head a few times, and I'm pretty sure the stunning tall lady was Amelie Lens, a Belgian tech-house DJ and former model. (She played that Primavera, too.) Lens is playing next year's Coachella, doing a back-to-back set with Sara Landry, another impossibly glamorous DJ.

Dance music, like so many other genres, used to be dominated by men to a baffling degree. Prominent female acts like DJ Rap were extremely rare. Those days seem to be over. The Coachella poster always has so many EDM acts, and I'm just now noticing that some of them — Peggy Gou, Charlotte de Witte, KI/KI — are women who look like movie stars. I didn't know this was happening, and I have no idea how to discuss it, but there it is.

16. Some of these people are very high on the poster. Congratulations to Dom Dolla, Empire Of The Sun, Jisoo, Role Model, Solomun, Solid Grooves, Snow Strippers, BOLO, Barry Can't Swim, Cloonee, Remi Wolf, Boy Harsher, Boris Brejcha, Pinegrove, Chris Stassy, Odd Mob, Franky Rizardo, and Vintage Culture. You're all a lot more popular than I realized. I'd never even heard of some of you. (Dance DJs, mostly. Same as it ever was.)

17. Some of these people should be a lot higher on the poster. I don't have any love in my heart for the Neighbourhood, but I thought they were an arena-level band, not a "billed under Four Tet" situation. (Congrats are also in order for Four Tet, who always seems to do well at these things.) I'm similarly confused about the poster placement for acts like Mike D, Leon Bridges, MUNA, Victoria Monét, the Avalanches, and Mariah The Scientist, all of whom probably deserve bigger font sizes than what they got. Tell your agents to get tougher!

18. The part of the column where we name some guys who could be playing the festival but aren't. Doechii! Fontaines D.C.! Tinashe! Hayley Williams! Wednesday! Atlas Sound! King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard! Sturgill Simpson! Cameron Winter! Ratboys! DIIV! Westside Cowboy! Nia Archives! Lime Garden! Grace Ives! Erika de Casier! Quiet Light! RIP Magic! Lip Critic! Sophia Stel! untitled (halo)! PISS, if you wanted to make everyone really uncomfortable! I guess maybe Drake!

19. Violet Grohl.

Honestly. Come on. Read the room. Same goes for you, Villanelle frontman Gene Gallagher.

entry.title: KATSEYE’s Megan Performs Seated And Wearing Sunglasses After Concussion
entry.summary: The chaotic KATSEYE saga continues: Last week, KATSEYE canceled shows due to Megan’s concussion. The girl group resumed their tour last night (Nov. 10) in Austin, and Megan was seated in a chair and wearing dark sunglasses for the duration of the performance. Viral videos show Megan perched toward the side of the stage while…
entry.content:
The chaotic KATSEYE saga continues: Last week, KATSEYE canceled shows due to Megan's concussion. The girl group resumed their tour last night (Nov. 10) in Austin, and Megan was seated in a chair and wearing dark sunglasses for the duration of the performance.

Viral videos show Megan perched toward the side of the stage while the rest of the group — Daniela, Lara, and Yoonchae, as Manon and Sophia are still on hiatus — sing and perform dance choreography. The videos are predictably very bleak, but Megan did sing some parts and at one point told the audience, "I'm so excited to be back on this stage. Thank you guys so much for showing me so much support — I'm feeling so much better."

Fans are outraged at the KATSEYE management — HYBE x Geffen Records — for seemingly forcing the tour to continue. On Monday (Nov. 9), Megan shared the following post about her health:

Wanted to give you a little update and let you know that while I'm feeling so much better, I am still actively recovering from my concussion so I'll need to take some precautions as I continue to heal.

For the Austin show, I'll be performing on a modified schedule. This means reduced choreography, less intense movement, and taking breaks as needed. I won't be going full out just yet! My doctors have recommended these limitations for now and I'll need to be reassessed before returning to unrestricted performances.

Watch clips below.

entry.title: Star’s Revenge – “Sea Shanty”
entry.summary: Star's Revenge, the band led by Sunflower Bean's Olive Faber and Geese's Emily Green, have shared the new song "Sea Shanty."
entry.content:
Star's Revenge move quickly. The quartet led by Sunflower Bean's Olive Faber and Geese guitarist Emily Green announced their sophomore album Star's Revenge II last week with the release of lead single "Don't Worry Dynamite," and the whole LP will be out by the end of the month. Today, they're giving us another preview in the form of the noisily ramshackle, irrepressibly tuneful rocker "Sea Shanty." Hear it below.

Star's Revenge will play a brief run of shows in support of the record at an end-of-year residency at Brooklyn's Hart Bar. Here are the dates for that:

12/28 - Brooklyn, NY @ Hart Bar w/ Jake Sinclair
12/29 - Brooklyn, NY @ Hart Bar w/ Shyness
12/30 - Brooklyn, NY @ Hart Bar w/ Talli Sow
12/31 - Brooklyn, NY @ Hart Bar w/ Burner Herzog

Star's Revenge II is out 11/27. Pre-order it here.

entry.title: Parent Teacher Announces New EP Celestial Mom: Hear “Eight Cents”
entry.summary: Tricks For Meds, Richard Spitzer’s recent album as Parent Teacher, was worth your time. So is “Eight Cents,” the lead single and opening track from his forthcoming EP Celestial Mom. The track maintains Spitzer’s knack for songcraft that feels classic yet idiosyncratic, bringing together drum machines with chorus-inflected guitars as he neurotically reflects on self-worth:…
entry.content:
Tricks For Meds, Richard Spitzer's recent album as Parent Teacher, was worth your time. So is "Eight Cents," the lead single and opening track from his forthcoming EP Celestial Mom. The track maintains Spitzer's knack for songcraft that feels classic yet idiosyncratic, bringing together drum machines with chorus-inflected guitars as he neurotically reflects on self-worth:

I spend a lot of time writing songs about how ridiculous the world has become, so I figured it was probably time to acknowledge that I’m part of the problem. "Eight Cents" is basically about wanting people to like you while simultaneously finding the whole idea of being liked kind of humiliating. I wanted it to sound upbeat, because there’s something inherently funny about having an existential crisis over a bunch of dad-rock riffs.

Listen below.

TRACKLIST:
01 "Eight Cents"  
02 "Daylight"
03 "Idiot"
04 "Keys To The Castle"

Celestial Mom is due out in the spring via Wilbur & Moore Records.
